opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's one of the most useful reference classes we have for thinking about how fast things could go after something like superintelligence, because it's a case where a whole society decided that producing a certain kind of thing was the overriding priority, and then we got to see what happened.

The US in World War II is the classic example. Around 1939 the US was producing a few thousand military aircraft a year, and by 1944 it was producing something like ninety-odd thousand. That's more than an order of magnitude in roughly four or five years. And they did it mostly by converting existing industry rather than building everything from scratch. The car companies stopped making cars and started making tanks, engines and planes. Ford built the Willow Run plant, and once it got going it was turning out B-24 bombers at something like one an hour. Liberty ships went from taking many months to build to being assembled in weeks, and as a publicity stunt they built one in under five days.

So the lessons I take from it are a few. First, existing productive capacity is surprisingly fungible. A factory that makes cars can be retooled to make something quite different within a year or two if people are really motivated. Second, learning curves are steep when you're doing something at scale and you care a lot about it. Costs and build times fell dramatically as they iterated. Third, and this is the most important part for me, this was all done by humans. It was humans figuring out the designs, humans managing the logistics, humans on the assembly lines, often newly trained ones, often people who had never worked in a factory before.

Now imagine the same kind of economy-wide push, but where the planning, the engineering, the management, and eventually the physical labor are being done by AI systems that are smarter than the best humans, that work around the clock, that can copy themselves, and that don't need years of training. That seems like it should go faster than the wartime mobilization, not slower. So when people tell me it would take decades to build out a robot economy after we get superintelligence, I point to this and say, look, ordinary humans with ordinary motivation and 1940s technology managed a tenfold scale-up in a few years. That gives you a sort of lower bound on what's possible, and the actual speed with superintelligence directing things could be considerably faster. Maybe a year or so to get to a million robots a year, something in that range, rather than many decades.

I should say there are real disanalogies. In wartime there was a lot of political will and the government was willing to override normal regulations and market processes, and you might not get that by default. But in an AI arms race scenario, especially one framed around competition with China, I think you actually could get something quite similar, which is part of what worries me.

r001.rationale: The response describes roughly a tenfold increase in aircraft production over four or five years. That is about one order of magnitude, not multiple orders of magnitude.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main thing it shows is that the binding constraint on how fast you can scale up production is usually not physics, it's motivation and coordination. In peacetime, factories get built on a timeline set by permitting, by financing, by nobody really wanting to take the risk of overbuilding. And then World War II happens and the United States goes from producing a few thousand aircraft a year to something like a hundred thousand a year within a few years. Shipyards that didn't exist in 1940 are cranking out Liberty ships in a matter of weeks per hull. Whole industries get repurposed — car plants making bombers, that kind of thing. And the thing to notice is that the underlying technology didn't change much in that window. What changed was that a lot of very capable people decided this was the most important thing in the world and the government was willing to pay for it and cut through the usual obstacles.

So when I think about AI and the question of how fast you could build out, say, data centres or chip fabs or robots, I'm not reasoning from the peacetime growth rates we see now. I'm asking: what happens if the people in charge come to believe this is existential, in the way that the war was? And historically the answer is that you can get a doubling of relevant output in a year or two, sometimes faster, across a sector that people previously thought was pretty sclerotic. There's a limit to that — you still have to pour concrete and it still has to cure, you still have to train people — but the limit is a lot higher than people's intuitions, because their intuitions are calibrated on a world where nobody's trying very hard.

And then the extra thing with AI is that the "motivated humans" piece might partially get replaced. If you've got AI systems that can do the engineering and the project management and eventually the physical work, then you're not even bounded by the number of people you can mobilise. That's where I think the wartime analogy actually undersells it. Wartime mobilisation is what humans can do when they're desperate. The scenario I worry about is one where you've got that level of urgency plus a labour force that's growing on a software timeline rather than a demographic one.

r001.rationale: The response describes rapid growth, including aircraft production rising from a few thousand to about 100,000 per year, but that is not multiple orders of magnitude. Its general claim is that output can double in a year or two.

astra-6.text:
I think it shows that production can scale surprisingly quickly when people are sufficiently motivated and willing to make tradeoffs. In peacetime, you might look at an industry’s growth rate and think that’s roughly the limit of what’s possible. But in wartime, governments put in enormous orders, companies convert factories, people work longer hours, and resources get diverted from other uses. And suddenly the trajectory looks very different.

That doesn’t mean you can produce anything you want overnight. You still need factories, machinery, raw materials, and trained workers. The lesson is that ordinary growth rates aren’t necessarily a good guide to how quickly production could expand under a concerted national effort. You have to look at the actual bottlenecks.

r001.rationale: The response says production can expand surprisingly quickly under a concerted national effort, but it does not state that ordinary humans can increase it by multiple orders of magnitude within a few years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it shows that you can get surprisingly rapid increases in production when people are sufficiently motivated. You can have a peacetime economy where building a new factory takes years, and then in wartime suddenly people find ways to do it much faster. They work around the clock, they simplify designs, they redirect resources, and they accept costs that wouldn’t normally seem worth paying.

The lesson isn’t that you can instantly produce an arbitrary amount of anything. There are still physical bottlenecks, and some things take time. But I think we should be wary of treating the speed at which we normally build things as a hard limit on how quickly we could build them under very different circumstances. In particular, if you’re imagining an AI boom, where there’s both an enormous economic incentive to expand production and potentially much better technology for doing so, ordinary industrial growth rates might be a pretty misleading guide.

r001.rationale: It describes production rising much faster under wartime motivation, but does not state an increase of multiple orders of magnitude within a few years.
